lesson.title: Where attention goes

steps.headline: Seeing needs attention, so something plainly visible can still go unnoticed.

lead.text: Selective attention lets you follow one stream and ignore the rest. In one famous study, viewers counted basketball passes and many never noticed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the game. This is inattentional blindness.
The object was in plain view. It was not attended, so it was not seen.
In a class demonstration, 30 people counted basketball passes. 14 of them failed to notice the person in the gorilla suit.

reveal.text: Nearly half missed it. Simons and Chabris reported 46% in the original study. In this class only 1 of 30 people who simply watched missed it.

steps.headline: Each change of task adds a switch cost while the mind reconfigures.

lead.text: Take two kinds of judgement: odd or even for digits (A), vowel or consonant for letters (B). Every trial takes some time, and every change from A to B or B to A adds a switch cost on top.
Total time = trials × time per trial + switches × switch cost.

steps.headline: Find the time for AABAB when each trial takes 400 ms and each switch adds 100 ms.

workedSteps.text: Count the changes of task: A to B, B to A, A to B.
Add the trial time and the switch time.

reveal.text: You counted seven changes in eight trials and added their cost to the trial time. Alternating is expensive because every trial after the first is a switch.

lead.text: Now use the digit and letter judgements. Each trial takes 600 ms, and each change of task adds 200 ms.
Now compare the same eight judgements done in two blocks, AAAABBBB, with the alternating order. The trial times and the switch cost are as before.

reveal.text: Alternating loses 1,200 ms. Preparation shrinks switch costs but does not remove them, which is why answering messages while writing is slower than it feels.

lead.text: Watson and Strayer tested 200 people driving a simulator while doing a demanding memory-and-arithmetic task. Doing two demanding tasks usually means alternating between them.

reveal.text: Only 5, or 2.5%, showed no measurable cost. They are called supertaskers. Most people who believe they multitask well are among the other 97.5%.

lesson.orientation: Measure what selective attention misses and what switching between tasks costs.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You have eight cards to sort, each one a different kind of job. Four are maths sums and four are word puzzles. Each card takes the same time to do. You can do the sums first and the words after, or swap every card between sum and word.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say why attending to one thing hides another, and work out what switching between tasks costs you in time.

recap.keyIdea: Attention is selective, so unattended things can be missed even when visible, and every change of task adds a switch cost. Multitasking is mostly alternating.

blocks.text: You found that 14 of 30 counters, 46.7%, missed the gorilla. Alternating ABABABAB took 6,200 ms against 5,000 ms in blocks, a 1,200 ms loss, and only 2.5% of drivers showed no cost.

recap.nextHook: Switching costs hint that the mind holds only a little at once. How little?

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 500 ms and each change of task adds 150 ms. How long does AABBAABB take, in milliseconds?
hints: Look for each place where A is followed by B or B by A.
There are eight trials at 500 ms each.
Add the switch costs to 4,000 ms.
questions.onCorrect: Trial time plus switch time, with only the changes of task counted as switches.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the trials. Add the cost of each change of task.
Read the sequence again. It changes task fewer times than that.

questions.prompt: An observer concentrating on a task fails to see a clearly visible but unexpected object. What is this failure called?
hints: It is a kind of blindness caused by where attention was directed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inattentional blindness: the object was visible but not attended.

questions.onCorrect: The object was visible but not attended, so it went unseen. That is inattentional blindness.

misconceptions.feedback: Change blindness is missing a change between two views. Here the object was never attended.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 500 ms and each change of task adds 150 ms. How many milliseconds faster is AAAABBBB than AABBAABB?
hints: Both have eight trials, so only the switches differ.
Count the switches in each sequence.
Multiply the difference in switches by the cost of one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AABBAABB has 3 switches and AAAABBBB has 1. The 2 extra switches cost 2 × 150 = 300 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Equal trials mean only switches differ: two extra switches at the same cost each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole switch cost of the mixed order. The blocked order has a switch too.
That is the cost of one switch. How many extra switches are there?

questions.prompt: Which order will take less time?
hints: Each card takes the same time. What else is going on between cards?
Think about what happens in your head each time the kind of job changes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sums first, then words: the job changes only once, so the mind reconfigures only once.

choices.label: Swapping between a sum and a word each time
They will take the same time.

questions.onCorrect: Changing job costs time on top of the work itself. You reasoned out a switch cost before it had a name.

misconceptions.feedback: Every swap makes you change the kind of job. That is extra work beyond the cards themselves.
The cards take equal time, but the changes between jobs do not come free.

questions.prompt: Which statement does inattentional blindness support?
hints: The object in the study was in plain view.

acceptedIdeas: Looking at something does not guarantee that you see it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Looking is not seeing: an object in plain view can be missed if attention is elsewhere.

choices.label: People with poor eyesight cannot see unexpected things.
Looking at something does not guarantee that you see it.

questions.onCorrect: Attention decides what you notice, so something in plain view can still be missed.

misconceptions.feedback: The viewers had ordinary eyesight. The cause was where their attention was.
Many did see it. It was missed only by those attending elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What percentage missed it? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide the number who missed it by the number watching.
The denominator is 30.
Convert 14/30 to a percentage and round to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 14/30 = 0.4667, or 46.7%, close to the 46% Simons and Chabris reported.

questions.onCorrect: Divide those who missed it by all who watched: nearly half failed to notice something in plain view.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of people who missed it. Turn it into a percentage of everyone watching.
That is the share who noticed it. The question asks for the share who missed it.

questions.prompt: How many switches are in the sequence ABBA?
hints: A switch is a change from one task to the other.
Read the sequence from left to right.
Count the places where the letter changes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A to B, then B to A: two switches. B to B is not a switch.

questions.onCorrect: A switch is a change of task: A to B and B to A. Repeating B costs nothing extra.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only one of the two changes. Read the sequence left to right.
That counts the gap between every pair of trials. Repeats are not switches.

questions.prompt: Why are there 3 switches in a sequence of 5 trials?
hints: Look at each pair of neighbouring trials. Is the task different?

acceptedIdeas: Only a change from one task to the other counts, and the first two trials are the same task.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only a change of task is a switch. Two As in a row are not.

choices.label: Every trial after the first counts as a switch.
Every second trial is a switch.
Only a change from one task to the other counts, and the first two trials are the same task.

questions.onCorrect: Only changes of task count. A repeated task adds no switch cost.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be four, and it ignores that the first two trials match.
Switches depend on the sequence, not on every other trial.

questions.prompt: How long does the sequence ABABABAB take in total, in milliseconds?
hints: Count the places where the letter changes.
Every trial costs 600 ms; each switch adds 200 ms.
Add 8 × 600 to the number of switches × 200.
questions.onCorrect: Trial time plus switch time: eight trials, and a switch before every trial except the first.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the trials. Each change of task adds more.
Eight trials make only seven changes. Count the gaps where the task changes.

questions.prompt: How many milliseconds longer does ABABABAB take than AAAABBBB?
hints: Both sequences have eight trials, so only switches differ.
Count the switches in each sequence.
Multiply the difference in switches by 200 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ABABABAB has 7 switches and AAAABBBB has 1; the extra 6 switches cost 6 × 200 = 1,200 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Both have eight trials, so only the switches differ: six more switches, each at the same cost.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost of one switch. How many more switches does the alternating order have?
That is the whole switch cost of the alternating order. The blocked order has a switch too.

questions.prompt: In the study, 5 of 200 drivers showed no cost from doing a demanding task while driving. What percentage is that?
hints: Divide the supertaskers by the total tested.
The total is 200.
Convert 5/200 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Five in two hundred is a very small share: nearly everyone paid a cost for doing two things.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of drivers. Turn it into a percentage of all those tested.
That is the share who showed a cost. The question asks about those who showed none.
